summaries.example: Suppose the sentence “The window is open” is true. A truthmaker would be something about the real window—such as its being open—that helps explain why the sentence is true. The sentence is a truthbearer: something that can be true or false. The truthmaker is not causing the sentence like a person causes an event. It is connected to the sentence because the sentence describes how things are.
summaries.summary: The truthmaker debate asks what connects true statements with reality. If “The bird is on the branch” is true, philosophers ask what makes it true. Perhaps it is the bird’s being there, a fact about the bird, or another kind of feature of the world. They also ask what can be a truthbearer: a sentence, a belief, or an abstract proposition. Several theories try to explain truthmaking. Entailment says that the existence of a truthmaker guarantees a truth, but this can make unrelated things count as truthmakers for necessary truths such as basic arithmetic. Necessitation uses a special relation between reality and truth, but it also needs to explain why irrelevant things should not count. An axiomatic approach describes truthmaking through connected principles instead of reducing it to one simpler idea. Grounding treats truthmaking as a kind of non-causal dependence. Philosophers also disagree about whether every truth needs a truthmaker, whether negative statements need special truthmakers, and whether truth merely depends on what exists. The entry presents these disagreements rather than settling them.
key_ideas: A truthmaker is what a truth is true because of, not what causes someone to say it.
One truth can have several truthmakers, and one truthmaker can help make several related truths true.
Some philosophers think every truth needs a truthmaker. Others think only certain truths do.
Proposed explanations include entailment, necessitation, principles, and grounding. Each has possible problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Truthmaking matters because it concerns how language and thought connect with the world. It asks whether truths are anchored in reality or can simply be accepted without anything behind them. This affects big questions about facts, mathematics, absence, possibility, and what exists. Learning about the debate also shows how philosophers test a theory: they look for helpful explanations, but they also check whether a theory counts too many unrelated things as explanations.

important_terms.definition: Something in reality that helps make a statement true. Philosophers disagree about exactly what kinds of things can play this role.
A sentence, belief, or proposition that can be true or false.
A relation of being true because of how something is, rather than being caused like an ordinary event.
The idea that a true statement depends on something that exists or happens in reality.

questions_to_think_about: What makes it true that your classroom has windows?
Could a true statement about something that does not exist have a truthmaker?
Is a math truth made true by objects in the world, or in some other way?
Should every true statement need something in reality to support it?

summaries.example: Consider the contingent proposition, “This apple is red.” A truthmaker theorist may say that some feature of reality—perhaps a fact involving this particular apple and redness—makes the proposition true. Merely having an apple, or merely having the property redness somewhere, may not be enough, since those things could exist without this apple being red. The example illustrates the demand for relevance: a truthmaker should be connected to what the proposition represents, not merely guarantee it through a loose logical or modal route.
summaries.summary: Truthmaker theory investigates the relation expressed when we say that something makes a proposition true. The central intuition is that truth should be connected to an independently existing reality, but the entry emphasizes that there is little agreement about the relation, the truthbearers involved, or the range of truths eligible for truthmakers. A definition in terms of entailment is attractive because entailment is familiar in logic, yet classical entailment makes any existing thing a truthmaker for every necessary truth. Adding relevance may block this result, but “aboutness” is difficult to define. Metaphysical necessitation instead proposes a cross-category relation between a worldly entity and a truthbearer. It avoids treating truthmaking as merely a relation between representations, but arguments for it can be circular, and cases involving irrelevant necessitation challenge its sufficiency. Questions about whether propositions have essentially fixed meanings also create tension for naturalistic views. The axiomatic approach treats truthmaking as governed by principles such as factivity, existence, and entailment, while remaining more metaphysically neutral. Grounding theories identify truthmaking with, or explain it through, non-causal metaphysical dependence. Their fine-grained character may avoid over-generation, though grounding is itself controversial and may require abstract propositions. The entry then examines maximalism, optimalism, negative and general truths, and the weaker claim that truth supervenes on being or subject matter. Finally, it considers motivations from realism, correspondence, explanatory adequacy, and the limits of theories that posit unsupported counterfactuals or dispositions.
key_ideas: The debate concerns several linked questions: what truthmaking is, which truths need it, what truthmakers are, why truthmakers are useful, and what truthbearers are.
A simple entailment account over-generates truthmakers: because necessary truths follow from anything, any existing object could become a truthmaker for them.
Necessitation avoids defining truthmaking solely as a relation between representations, but it faces worries about relevance, circular arguments, internal relations, and the nature of propositions.
An axiomatic theory gives principles governing truthmaking without necessarily reducing it to a more basic relation; its principles still require careful interpretation.
Grounding may offer a fine-grained, unified account of non-causal dependence, but grounding itself is contested and may commit a theory to abstract propositions.
Maximalism, optimalism, and subject-matter views disagree about whether negative and general truths need truthmakers of their own.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue matters to metaphysics because it asks what, if anything, anchors true representations in reality. It bears on realism, the status of facts and propositions, the treatment of negative and universal claims, and the contrast between necessary and contingent truth. It also illustrates a general philosophical problem: a theory can be too weak to explain dependence, but too strong if it counts irrelevant entities as truthmakers. The debate therefore connects logical form, ontology, modality, explanation, and the limits of reduction.

important_terms.definition: That in virtue of which a truthbearer is true; the term is meant to describe a non-causal connection between reality and truth.
A sentence, belief, proposition, or other representational item that is capable of being true or false.
A relation in which one representation guarantees another. Using it to define truthmaking risks making every existing thing a truthmaker for necessary truths.
A proposed metaphysical relation in which something in reality guarantees that a truthbearer is true. Critics ask whether it is sufficiently relevant and non-circular.
A non-causal dependence relation, often used to explain why one fact holds because of another.
The view that every truth has something in the world that makes it true.
The view that only some truths require truthmakers, aiming to preserve a connection with reality without positing one for every truth.
The idea that changes in truth require corresponding changes in what the truth is about, without necessarily requiring truthmakers as entities.

questions_to_think_about: Does the existence of an object entail every necessary truth, and if so, should that make the object a truthmaker?
Can a theory explain why a truth depends on reality without identifying a truthmaker?
Are negative truths true because something exists, because something is absent, or because no positive truthmaker exists for the opposite?
Would a theory that uses grounding explain truthmaking, or merely replace one difficult concept with another?
Does the intuition that truth depends on being support maximalism, or only a weaker subject-matter principle?

summaries.example: Imagine that the statement “There are no dragons in the school library” is true. One philosopher might look for a special fact or condition in the library that makes the statement true. Another might say it is true because there is no truthmaker for the opposite statement, “A dragon is in the library.” A third might say that the statement depends on the library and its contents, without requiring a special object called a “no-dragons fact.” The example shows why negative truths are especially difficult for truthmaker theories.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the philosophical idea that truths have truthmakers: things in reality in virtue of which truthbearers are true. The idea is not causal. A potter makes a pot, but a truthmaker is supposed to support a truth by the way reality is related to what the truthbearer says. The debate begins with questions about the nature of truthmaking and truthbearers, then considers several accounts. Entailment makes truthmaking depend on a logical guarantee, but classical entailment threatens to make every object a truthmaker for necessary truths. Necessitation introduces a metaphysical relation between reality and truth, yet philosophers question whether it is relevant enough, whether arguments for it are circular, and whether its truthbearers must be special propositions. The axiomatic approach states principles governing truthmaking without reducing it to a single deeper concept. Grounding treats truthmaking as a type of non-causal dependence, though the nature of grounding is disputed. The entry also compares maximalism, which gives every truth a truthmaker, with optimalism, which gives the role only to selected truths. Negative and general truths are central tests: proposed answers include negative facts, totality facts, the absence of truthmakers for opposite claims, and weaker supervenience principles. The larger motivation is the thought that truth should depend on how reality is, though some philosophers think subject matter or explanation can capture this without truthmakers.
key_ideas: Truthmaker theories try to explain how true statements are tied to a reality that is not itself merely a representation.
Philosophers disagree about whether truthmakers are objects, facts, properties, states of affairs, or something else.
Classical entailment has a surprising consequence: any existing thing entails necessary truths, such as arithmetic truths, even when it seems irrelevant.
Negative truths and general truths create special challenges because it is hard to identify what makes “nothing is F” or “everything is F” true.
Maximalists require truthmakers for all truths; optimalists restrict the requirement, especially for negative and general statements.
Grounding and supervenience offer alternative ways to describe dependence, but they may not fully explain the direction or mechanism of that dependence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Truthmaker theory matters because it connects everyday statements with deep questions about reality. It asks whether a true claim needs something outside language and thought to account for its truth. The debate helps clarify why negative claims, universal claims, mathematics, and necessary truths are difficult. It also teaches an important philosophical lesson: two people may agree that truth depends on reality while disagreeing sharply about what that dependence is and what entities, if any, are required.

important_terms.definition: Something in reality that makes a sentence, belief, or proposition true, although not by causing it in the ordinary sense.
A sentence, belief, or proposition that can be true or false.
A logical connection in which one claim guarantees another claim. A theory based on it may count too many things as truthmakers.
A proposed relation in which something in the world guarantees that a truth is true in every relevant possibility.
A non-causal relation of dependence: one fact is true because of another fact or feature of reality.
The position that every truth has a truthmaker.
The position that only some truths need truthmakers, while still keeping a connection between truth and reality.
A weaker view that truth varies with the things a statement is about, without always requiring a separate truthmaker.

questions_to_think_about: If a claim is necessarily true, should every existing object count as one of its truthmakers?
What could make a negative statement true if the thing it mentions does not exist?
Is “truth depends on reality” stronger than saying that truth changes when its subject matter changes?
Can a theory remain neutral about what truthbearers are?
Which seems more convincing: maximalism, optimalism, or a subject-matter view?
